extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers studying algebraic geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Excerpts from a graduate-level algebraic geometry textbook giving theorem statements, desiderata, and exercises about Stein factorization, Zariski's Main Theorem, resolution of singularities for curves, Castelnuovo's criterion for (−1)-curves, the Theorem on Formal Functions, and Serre duality. Intended to state precise conditions and guide proofs/constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolution of singularities for curves — arithmetic genus criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: To desingularize a reduced projective curve C over a field k by successive blow-ups one uses the arithmetic genus pa as an integer invariant. One must show (i) if pa(C) = pa(˜C) then ν is an isomorphism (C already nonsingular); (ii) if C' → C is birational then pa(C) ≥ pa(C') (so pa(˜C) is a lower bound throughout the process); and (iii) blowing up a singular point decreases the arithmetic genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: For a finite morphism π : C' → C that is an isomorphism away from a finite set, OC → π_*OC' has cokernel G supported on finitely many closed points; χ(C',OC') = χ(C,OC) + χ(C,G) so pa(C) ≥ pa(C') with equality iff π is O-connected (G = 0). Use these facts to show blow-ups decrease pa and so the algorithm of blowing up singular points terminates. Exercises and hints: verify the exact sequence 0 → OC → π_*OC' → G → 0, use vanishing Hi(C,G)=0 for i>0, and apply Zariski’s Connectedness Lemma where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: O-connectedness of proper birational morphisms (exercise 29.5.B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose π : X → Y is a proper morphism of locally Noetherian schemes that is an isomorphism over a dense open subset of Y and Y is normal. Then π is O-connected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Application: blow-ups of smooth varieties under smooth centers satisfy this. Use Zariski’s Connectedness Lemma 29.5.1 for connectedness of fibers and properties of normalization; see hint: Exercise 9.7.P. This criterion is used to deduce that certain birational contractions are O-connected, which is an ingredient in arguments like resolution or uniqueness of contractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness of contraction determined by contracted locus (exercise 29.5.C)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two proper morphisms π : X → Y and π' : X → Y' of locally Noetherian schemes each contract the same connected set of X (and are isomorphisms elsewhere), and Y and Y' are normal, then π and π' are the same (more precisely, there is an isomorphism i : Y → Y' such that π' = i ◦ π).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hint: Identify Y and Y' as topological spaces (their underlying topologies are determined by the contracted locus) and then recover the structure sheaves using Stein factorization/π_*OX to show the maps agree as morphisms of schemes. This gives uniqueness of contractions determined purely by the locus contracted on X.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stein factorization commutes with flat base change
rubrics_metrics.description: The construction of the Stein factorization of a morphism of locally Noetherian schemes commutes with any flat base change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the functorial nature of π_* and formation of Spec of the pushforward algebra; flat base change preserves formation of π_* and finiteness properties, so the factorization (X → X0 → Y with X0 = Spec π_*OX and X → X0 O-connected, X0 → Y finite) is compatible with base change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zariski's Main Theorem (Grothendieck's form, Theorem 29.6.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) For a proper morphism π : X → Y of locally Noetherian schemes, the set X0 ⊂ X of points that are isolated in their fiber is open. (b) The restriction π|X0 factors as an open embedding followed by a finite morphism: there exists Y' and factorization X0 → Y' (open immersion) → Y (finite).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategy: take the Stein factorization X → Y' → Y, reduce to the O-connected case where fibers are connected, identify X0 with the unramified locus Ω_{α}=0 for the O-connected factor α, and use properties of Ω to show openness. Detailed hints and exercise references (e.g., reduction to varieties using upper semicontinuity) are given in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion: point isolated in fiber ⇔ Ω_{α}|_p = 0 (exercise 29.6.A)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the O-connected factor α in Stein factorization, a point p ∈ X is isolated in its fiber of α iff the sheaf of differentials Ω_{α} vanishes at p (i.e., (Ω_{α})_p = 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: the unramified locus (where Ω vanishes) coincides with the locus of isolated points in fibers for proper O-connected morphisms. Use localization and properties of Ω to check equivalence; this identification is used to prove openness of X0 in Zariski's Main Theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of finite morphisms (Theorem 29.6.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a morphism π : X → Y of locally Noetherian schemes the following are equivalent: (a) π is finite; (b) π is affine and proper; (c) π is proper and quasi-finite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketch: (a) ⇒ (b) is by definition and standard properties. To get (b)⇒(c) show affine proper morphisms have finite fibers. For (c)⇒(a) apply Zariski's Main Theorem to get a factorization X0 (open) → Y' (finite) → Y and use Cancellation Theorem for proper morphisms to show π is finite. See Exercises referenced for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nagata compactification hypothesis (†)
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π : X → Y of locally Noetherian schemes satisfies (†) if for some open cover {U_i} of Y by affines, each restriction π|_{π^{-1}(U_i)} factors as an open embedding into a scheme proper over U_i. Such a morphism is necessarily separated and finite type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nagata's Compactification Theorem: every separated finite type morphism of Noetherian schemes satisfies (†) (i.e., can be factored as an open embedding into a scheme proper over the base). References and hints for removing Noetherian hypotheses (quasicompact/quasiseparated) are noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quasi-finite morphisms as open subsets of finite morphisms (exercise 29.6.E)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose π : X → Y is a quasi-finite morphism of Noetherian schemes satisfying (†). Then π factors as an open embedding into a finite morphism Y' → Y (i.e., X → Y factors as X → Y' (open) → Y (finite)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formalizes the heuristic that quasi-finite morphisms are 'open subsets of finite morphisms'. Use Zariski’s Main Theorem and the (†) hypothesis; see Exercise 7.3.15 for related statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Castelnuovo's Criterion for contracting (−1)-curves (Theorem 29.7.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let C ⊂ X be a (−1)-curve on a smooth projective surface X over a field k. Then there exists a birational morphism π : X → Y with Y a smooth projective surface, π(C) a k-valued point, π the blow-up of Y at that point, and C the exceptional divisor of the blow-up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof outline given in three steps: (1) construct an invertible sheaf L (via L = H(kC) for suitable very ample H with H^1(X,H)=0) whose complete linear series contracts C to a point; (2) show the image Y is smooth at the contraction point using the Theorem on Formal Functions and identifying completed local ring with k[[x,y]]; (3) use universal property of blow-up and that C is an effective Cartier divisor to identify π with Bl_q Y. Exercises 29.7.A–G give the detailed properties needed (vanishing, base-point-freeness, contraction, finiteness of fibers). Uniqueness of contraction follows from earlier exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of an invertible sheaf L = H(kC) with vanishing H^1 properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a very ample invertible sheaf H on X with H^1(X,H)=0 and take k large so that H^1(X, H(iC)) = 0 for 0 ≤ i ≤ k; define L := H(kC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Serre vanishing and properties of very ample sheaves (Exercise 16.6.C and Theorem 18.1.4(ii)) to find such H and k. Then show L is base-point-free (Exercise 29.7.B), that the associated morphism contracts C to a point and is an embedding away from C (Exercise 29.7.C), and use degree computations on C ≅ P^1 to verify deg L|_C = 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion: blow-up is isomorphism ⇒ point nonsingular (exercise 29.5.E)
rubrics_metrics.description: If β : C' → C is the blow-up of a curve C at a point p and β is an isomorphism, then C is nonsingular at p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: if β is an isomorphism then the exceptional divisor is effective Cartier and p is cut out locally by a single equation; hence the local ring OC,p is principal and is a 1-dimensional regular local ring. Use Zariski’s Connectedness Lemma and identification of ringed spaces as indicated in the exercise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal surface definition and termination via Picard number
rubrics_metrics.description: A surface is minimal if it has no (−1)-curves. If not minimal, choose a (−1)-curve and blow it down; blowing down reduces the Picard number ρ by 1 (Exercise 22.4.O), and since ρ is finite this process terminates, yielding a minimal model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remarks: minimal models need not be unique; the text sketches known phenomena (e.g., P1×P1 and P2 examples) and references for classification. Use the finiteness of the Picard number and the Picard-number-decreasing property to justify termination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem on Formal Functions (29.8.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose X → Spec B is proper with B Noetherian and F is a coherent sheaf on X. Let I be an ideal of B, ^B the I-adic completion, Xn = X ×_B (B/I^{n+1}), and Fn the pullback of F to Xn. Then for all i the natural map Hi(X,F) ⊗_B ^B ← lim_{←} Hi(Xn,Fn) is an isomorphism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof outline: reinterpret Hi(Xn,Fn) as Hi(X, F/InF), analyze exact sequences 0 → InF → F → F/InF → 0 and take limits. Two key tasks: (i) show images of restriction maps im(u_n) are cofinal with the I-adic topology on Hi(X,F) using the Rees algebra R = ⊕ I^m and coherence of appropriate pushforwards; (ii) show kernels ker(v_n) stabilize in the sense that ker(v_{n+d}) = I^d ker(v_n) for large d (again via graded R-module finiteness and Proposition 12.9.2). Conclude using completion properties of finitely generated modules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serre duality desideratum: dualizing sheaf equals determinant of cotangent bundle for smooth varieties (30.1.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For smooth varieties X one desires ω_X (the dualizing sheaf) = K_X = det Ω_X; in particular ω_X should be an invertible sheaf (canonical bundle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is described as a desideratum that is harder to prove; the text promises to show ω_X is invertible in certain cases (e.g., regular embedding into a smooth variety, Exercise 30.4.H) and indicates Exercise 30.4.I and Corollary 30.3.10 combine to give earlier (Theorem 18.5.1) statements. The statement is highlighted as the expected dualizing object in Serre duality for smooth schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serre duality for vector bundles — functorial form (30.1.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If F is locally free of finite rank on a projective k-scheme X of pure dimension n, then there should be a functorial isomorphism Hi(X,F) ≅ H^{n−i}(X, F^∨ ⊗ ω_X)^∨, i.e., a perfect pairing functorial in F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explains construction via cup product and a trace map t : H^n(X,ω_X) → k; the functorial form is equivalent to producing a natural perfect pairing H^{n−i}(X, F^∨ ⊗ ω_X) × H^i(X,F) → k. The functorial version will be proved (Corollary 30.3.10) at least when X is Cohen–Macaulay (in particular smooth). The trace version (via cup product) is also discussed and indicated how it yields the functorial version.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serre duality for vector bundles — trace/cup-product version
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct a cup product Hi(X,F) × H^{n−i}(X, F^∨ ⊗ ω_X) → H^n(X, ω_X) and combine with a trace map t : H^n(X,ω_X) → k to obtain a perfect pairing Hi(X,F) × H^{n−i}(X, F^∨ ⊗ ω_X) → k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the operational form of Serre duality used to produce the isomorphism in the functorial form. The text notes the trace version holds when X is Cohen–Macaulay (and smooth); an indication of proof for this version is given in a later remark (30.3.15).

rubrics_metrics.name: Serre duality for Hom (30.1.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any coherent sheaf F on a pure n-dimensional projective k-scheme X there is a functorial isomorphism Hom(F, ω_X) ≅ H^n(X,F)^∨, with the natural pairing Hom(F,ω_X) × H^n(X,F) → H^n(X,ω_X) →^t k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a weaker but broadly applicable form of Serre duality (functorial Serre duality for Hom). The text presents the natural candidate pairing and indicates this is what will be proved without Cohen–Macaulay hypotheses. The trace map t : H^n(X,ω_X) → k again plays a central role.
